draft.title: Generating ideas
card: Brainstorming
Jot down many ideas fast, such as words, questions or links, without judging them. You choose the best ones afterwards.
Freewriting
Write without stopping for a set time, such as five minutes. Do not fix mistakes or cross anything out. An idea often turns up in the middle of the mess.
Borrowed first line
Start with a line from another writer, or a line you invent, and continue it in your own direction. Then you can delete the borrowed line.
Starting from an image
Pick a vivid picture, such as a photo or an object, and write what you see, who is there and what might happen next.
draft.remember: Ideas are found by trying things: list, write freely, borrow a start or look closely at an image.

a.q: Zara sets a timer for five minutes and writes without stopping, leaving every mistake in place. Which method is she using?
a.why: Writing nonstop for a set time without fixing anything is freewriting. Brainstorming is similar, but it is a quick list of separate ideas rather than continuous writing.
a.clue: She is writing in full, without stopping.

b.q: Leo has no idea for a short story. He looks at a photo of an empty train platform at night and writes who might be waiting and why. Which method is he using?
b.why: Leo begins from a picture and builds a story out of what he sees and imagines. It is not freewriting, because he is not writing nonstop with no focus. The photo is what gives him his idea.

problems.detail: The 'Borrowed first line' entry says the line can be 'a line you invent'. An invented line is not borrowed, which blurs what the method is.
Why (b) says freewriting is writing 'nonstop with no focus'. The card does not say freewriting has no focus; it only says to write without stopping for a set time without fixing mistakes.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. The card's 'borrowed first line' entry confusingly includes a line you invent, and why (b) describes freewriting as having 'no focus', which the card does not say.
